en: Because of the assault of the threefold suffering, there arises a desire to know the means of its removal. If it is argued that this [desire] is useless since a remedy is seen in the world, we say no, because such remedies are neither certain nor final. (ISk 1)
The scriptural method is like the perceptible one, for it is impure and characterized by decay and excess;
the opposite of that is superior, arising from the discriminative knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower. (ISk 2)
Root-nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolved;
the group of sixteen is only evolved; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolved. (ISk 3)
Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony—these three types of valid cognition are accepted because all means of knowledge are established by them;
for the establishment of the objects of knowledge depends upon valid cognition.

Perception is the ascertainment of each respective object; inference is declared to be threefold, preceded by the mark and that which possesses the mark; and authoritative verbal testimony is the word of a reliable person. (ISk 5)
However, from general observation, the cognition of supersensible things arises through inference;
and that which remains unestablished even by that [inference], being beyond perception, is to be proven through authoritative scripture.
Due to excessive distance, extreme proximity, impairment of the sense organs, instability of the mind, subtlety, obstruction, being overwhelmed, and merging with similar things. (ISk 7)
Its non-perception is due to its subtlety, not due to its non-existence; it is perceived through its effects.
And that effect, beginning with the Great One (mahat), is both dissimilar and similar to its primal cause (prakṛti).
Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, because not everything is possible from everything,
because an efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity, and because the effect exists in the cause, the effect is pre-existent.
The manifest is caused, impermanent, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composite, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite.

The manifest and the primal nature (pradhāna) consist of the three qualities, are non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive; the person (puruṣa), however, is the opposite of these.

The *guṇas* consist of pleasure, pain, and dejection; they serve the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint; and they function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship. (ISK 12)
Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping. Their functioning is for the sake of a purpose, like a lamp.

The properties of non-discrimination and so forth are established because [the manifest] consists of the three guṇas, because their opposites are absent [in the unmanifest], and because the effect possesses the nature of the qualities of its cause; thus, the Unmanifest is also established.

Because of the finite measure of diverse objects, because of their commonality, because of their activity proceeding from power, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe, [the Primal Cause exists]. (ISk 15)
The unmanifest cause exists; it proceeds from the three qualities (guṇas) and from their combination;
it evolves like water due to the specific distinctions of the substrates of each respective quality. ISk_16 //

The Puruṣa exists because the composite is for the sake of another, because of the reversal of the three guṇas and so forth, because of superintendence, because of the state of being an enjoyer, and because of activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya).

The plurality of Puruṣas is established from the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments [of action], from their non-simultaneous activity, and also from the diversity of the three guṇas. (ISk 18)
And from this absence of error, the witnesshood of this Puruṣa is established, as well as his isolation, neutrality, the state of being a seer, and the condition of non-agency. (ISk 19)
Therefore, through union with that [Self], the insentient *liṅga* appears as if it were sentient;
likewise, although the qualities (*guṇas*) are the agents, the indifferent [Self] appears as if it were the agent. (ISk 20)
For the purpose of the Puruṣa’s perception and for the sake of liberation of the Pradhāna, there is a union of both, like that of the lame and the blind; from that union, creation proceeds.
From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
and from five among that group of sixteen, the five gross elements arise.
Intellect is determination; it consists of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—this is its form when characterized by sattva; when characterized by tamas, it is the opposite of this.
Egoity is self-conceit; from it proceeds a twofold creation:
the elevenfold group of the senses and the fivefold group of subtle elements. (ISk 24)
The group of eleven [senses] proceeds from the *vaikṛta* (modifying) ego as *sāttvika*;
the subtle elements proceed from the *bhūtādi* (originative) ego as *tāmasa*; and from the *taijasa* (activating) ego, both arise.
The sense organs are known as hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell;
they say that speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals are the organs of action.
In this context, the mind possesses a dual nature; it is both the faculty of volition and a sense organ due to its common characteristics.
Its diversity arises from the specific modifications of the *guṇas* and from the distinction between its objects of perception. (ISk 27)
Regarding forms and the other [objects], the activity of the five [senses] is held to be mere observation;
however, speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure belong to the five [action organs].
The specific functioning of these three is unique;
the general functioning of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa. (ISk 29)

For the operation of the fourfold [means of knowledge] is taught to be both simultaneous and successive; likewise, when the object is perceived, the operation of the other three is preceded by that [perception]. Even when the object is unperceived, the operation of the three is preceded by that [perception].
Each [organ] adopts its own respective mode of activity, which is caused by the mutual intentions [of the organs];
the purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause, for no instrument is set in motion by anything else.
The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it performs the functions of grasping, maintaining, and manifesting. Its object is tenfold: that which is to be grasped, maintained, and manifested.
The internal organ is threefold; the external is tenfold and is called the object of the [internal] triad.
The external organ functions in the present time, while the internal organ functions in all three times.
Among those, the five sense organs have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific;
speech has sound as its object, while the remaining [four] also have the five [elements] as their objects.
Since the intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), penetrates every object,
therefore the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper, while the remaining ones are the gates.
These specific qualities, which are like lamps and distinct from one another,
having illuminated the entire purpose of the Puruṣa, present it to the intellect.

Since it is the intellect (buddhi) that accomplishes every object of experience for the person (puruṣa), and since it is that very intellect which distinguishes [the person from matter], it follows that the subtle difference between the primary matter (pradhāna) and the person exists.
The subtle elements (tanmātras) are the non-specific (aviśeṣa); from those five [subtle elements] arise the five gross elements (bhūtas).
These are known as the specific (viśeṣa), being calm, terrible, and deluded.
The subtle [beings], those born of mother and father, and those together with the gross—these are the three kinds of distinctions.
Among them, the subtle are constant; those born of mother and father cease.

The subtle body (liṅga), which has arisen previously, is unattached, constant, and extends from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the subtle elements; it transmigrates, devoid of enjoyment, yet permeated by dispositions (bhāva).

Just as a painting cannot exist without its support, and just as a shadow cannot exist without a post or other such object, so too the subtle body (liṅga) does not remain without its specific qualities (viśeṣas), being without a basis.

This subtle body (liṅga) functions like an actor, through the connection between causes and their effects, driven by the purpose of the Spirit (puruṣārtha), due to its association with the sovereignty of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Innate dispositions such as virtue (dharma) and the like are seen to depend upon the instruments (the senses), while those arising from nature or transformation,
such as the embryo (kalala) and so forth, depend upon the body (the effect).
Through dharma there is upward movement; through adharma, downward movement occurs.
Through knowledge comes liberation, while from its opposite, bondage is held to arise.

Through dispassion comes dissolution into primordial nature; through passionate attachment, worldly existence arises from the quality of rajas. Through sovereign power there is absence of obstruction; from its opposite, the reverse occurs.
This is the evolution of the intellect (pratyayasarga), known as error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment;
through the mutual suppression of the imbalance of the qualities (guṇas), its subdivisions number fifty.
There are five varieties of error, and twenty-eight varieties of incapacity due to the deficiency of the instruments; contentment is ninefold, and attainment is eightfold.
The division of *tamas* is eightfold, that of *moha* is likewise, and *mahāmoha* is tenfold;
*tāmisra* is eighteenfold, and so too is *andhatāmisra*.
The incapacitation of the eleven faculties, together with the incapacitation of the intellect, is designated as "incapacity" (aśakti);
there are seventeen such incapacitations of the intellect resulting from the inversion of contentment (tuṣṭi) and attainment (siddhi).

The four internal contentments are known as those consisting of nature, acquisition, time, and fortune; the external ones are said to be nine, arising from the cessation of the [five] objects of the senses. ISk 50.

Reasoning, oral instruction, study, the three-fold destruction of suffering, acquisition of friends, and generosity—these are the eight accomplishments; that which precedes accomplishment is the three-fold restraint.
There is no gender-sign without entities, nor is there the manifestation of entities without a gender-sign;
therefore, creation is twofold, consisting of that which is called gender and that which is called entity.
The divine creation is of eight kinds, that of animals is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; such, in brief, is the elemental creation.
The creation is vast in *sattva* at its summit, vast in *tamas* at its root,
and vast in *rajas* in the middle, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
In this regard, the conscious person experiences suffering caused by old age and death as long as the subtle body has not ceased; therefore, in brief, there is suffering.

Thus, this undertaking of Prakṛti—beginning with Mahat and ending with the objects of the senses—is for the sake of the liberation of each individual Puruṣa; though for the sake of another, it is as if it were for her own sake.
Just as the flow of milk from an insentient source occurs for the sake of the growth of the calf,
so too does the activity of the Pradhāna occur for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.
Just as people engage in activities for the sake of satisfying their longing,
so too does the Unmanifest engage [in the creation of the world] for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.
Just as a dancer ceases from her dance after displaying herself to the audience,
so does primordial nature (prakṛti) cease once she has manifested herself to the Spirit (puruṣa).
Through various means, she who has been helpful acts for the sake of that man who is ungrateful,
virtuous for one who is devoid of virtue, and pursues what is meaningless for him.
"It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than Prakṛti, which, once seen, does not present herself for sight again to the Puruṣa. (ISk 61)
Therefore, no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate;
rather, it is *prakṛti*, depending on various substrates, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated.
In this way, Nature binds herself to herself by means of the seven forms; and she alone, through a single form, liberates herself for the sake of the Puruṣa.
Thus, from the practice of reality, there arises the complete, unerring, and pure knowledge that "I am not," "nothing is mine," and "I do not exist"— a knowledge that is absolute.
Therefore, the Puruṣa, established like a spectator and remaining self-abiding, beholds Prakṛti, whose productivity has ceased and who has desisted from the seven forms by the power of the goal.
Upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, when [the causes] such as merit and so forth have ceased to function as causes,
he remains with his body sustained by the force of residual impressions, like the whirling of a potter's wheel.
When the dissolution of the body has occurred and the primary cause (pradhāna) has ceased its activity because its purpose has been fulfilled,
one attains both the certain and the absolute state of isolation (kaivalya).
This secret knowledge of the goals of human existence has been fully declared by the Supreme Seer;
herein, the stability, origin, and dissolution of all beings are contemplated.
The Sage, out of compassion, bestowed this supreme purifier upon Āsuri; Āsuri, in turn, gave it to Pañcaśikha, and by him the Tantra was extensively propagated.
This [treatise], which has come down through a succession of disciples, was composed in Āryā verses by Īśvarakṛṣṇa,
who had correctly understood the established doctrine with his noble intellect.
It is said that the seventy topics contained therein are the topics of the entire *Ṣaṣṭitantra*,
excluding the illustrative narratives and devoid of the arguments of opponents.
Therefore, this scripture, though seen in an abbreviated form, is not deficient in meaning;
it is like the reflection of the vast body of the Tantra appearing within a mirror.
